title: The Outfit Brief Starts With You
subtitle: Adaptive style is not one look or a list of special closures. Start with the wearer’s routine, access needs and aesthetic priorities—and use that brief to make clothing work without giving up what feels like you.
imageAlt: Two women partners compare jackets in front of a mirror, each wearing a different silhouette and pointing out details that suit her own style.
imageConcept: A warm, natural-light scene of two women partners co-styling outfits at home. Each has a distinct silhouette, color palette and personal preference; they are sharing ideas, not representing a particular disability or access need.
body: Style begins with the person wearing it

A useful outfit is not simply one that looks right on a hanger. It has to work in the circumstances where someone will wear it: sitting, standing, moving through a day, managing a fastening, or living with a fabric feel that is distracting. And it should still feel like their clothes—not a uniform prescribed by a practical problem. Adaptive clothing can include garments designed for access, existing pieces adjusted by a tailor, or familiar clothes chosen with a particular routine in mind. None of those routes has to define someone’s whole wardrobe. The first step is not to search for a universal solution. It is to describe what this wearer wants.
Write a three-line brief before browsing

Keep the exercise short enough to use. Write: **Where and how will I wear it?** Include the occasion, posture, movement or routine that matters. **What needs to work differently?** Name a specific issue such as reaching a closure, avoiding pressure, getting a garment on or off, or making room for something worn or used. **What do I want to keep?** Choose a color, silhouette, mood, coverage or other detail you do not want practical changes to erase. The answers can be brief: “Dinner with friends, mostly seated”; “less twisting to fasten”; “keep the sharp collar and deep green.” This is not a test of how well someone can explain a need. It is a reference point for comparing options.
Turn a general difficulty into a garment question

Specific questions make shopping and alterations more useful. Instead of “this shirt is hard,” ask where the difficulty happens: Is the armhole restrictive? Is the placket awkward to manage? Does the hem shift when sitting? Is the fabric uncomfortable against the skin? The answer may point toward a different cut, a closure change, a softer material, or simply another garment. A study of shirt design for 51 female wheelchair users examined changes including armholes, sleeve caps, plackets and fabric selection, with attention to seated reach and dressing convenience [2]. That is evidence that construction details can matter—not a prescription that every wheelchair user needs the same shirt. Treat the feature as a prompt to test what matters for one body and one routine.
Make comfort and access part of the style brief

Sensory comfort deserves the same clear language as fit. A seam, label, texture, pressure point or temperature may determine whether an outfit feels wearable. The article abstract reports that individuals with tactile defensiveness are dissatisfied with clothing and suggests occupational therapists partner with designers to develop tactile sensory-friendly clothes [1]. Its practical lesson is still useful: don’t assume that a functional garment is automatically comfortable, or that comfort requires abandoning personal style. If you know a fabric or feature is a problem, write it down in plain terms and use that information to screen options.
Check the fit in the position that matters

A garment can feel different as the body moves or changes position. If the outfit is mainly for sitting, check it while seated: notice the waist, hem, back, sleeves and any pulling or bunching. If dressing involves reaching, bending or limited hand movement, assess the relevant step at a comfortable pace. Try the garment over the layers you expect to wear, and include the shoes, mobility aid or other items that are part of the actual outfit if the wearer wants to. Fit checks should follow the wearer’s real use, not an imagined standard body.

Practical details can quietly take over a shopping conversation. A person may start looking for an easy closure, then find that every option feels too clinical, too plain or unlike what they would normally choose. That is why the third line of the brief—what to keep—matters. Make it concrete: a strong shoulder, a long line, a bright print, a particular neckline, a polished feel. Then compare choices against both the access need and the aesthetic priority. A modification does not have to be invisible, either. A visible contrast closure or altered hem can become part of the design if the wearer likes it. The standard is not whether a change looks “normal.” It is whether the person wants to wear it.
Compare ready-made clothes, adaptations and alterations

Once the brief is clear, compare routes rather than assuming there is one correct category of garment. Ready-made clothes may already meet the need. An adaptive garment may offer a construction feature that is hard to add later. A tailor or alterations professional may be able to adjust a favorite piece. The University of Delaware’s *Adaptive Clothing Resources* manual, developed through 41 interviews with people who had arm or hand difficulties dressing, covers garment features and fasteners as general educational information—not a substitute for professional guidance [3]. For an alteration, ask what can be changed, what the change might affect, and whether the garment can be tried or adjusted before the work is final. If a support person helps, make their role practical: hold options, take notes or brainstorm when invited. The wearer keeps the priorities.
Use the brief in the fitting room—and revise it

Bring the three lines on a phone or scrap of paper. Try one option at a time and check it against the brief: Can I wear it for the intended situation? Does the part that needed to work differently now feel manageable? Does it still look and feel like something I chose? If the answer is mixed, identify what is working and what is not before moving on. A small adjustment may be enough; sometimes the right decision is to leave the garment behind. The brief can change as routines, preferences or available options change. It is not a permanent label or a demand to optimize every outfit. It is a way to keep the conversation anchored in the wearer’s own definition of a good fit: access, comfort and style, considered together.
